extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media watchdogs, television decency, and conservative advocacy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the criteria and standards used by the Parents Television Council (PTC) to judge television and other entertainment media for family-appropriateness; includes their stated mission, content standards, measurement practices, policy proposals, and advocacy tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTC mission: promote responsibility and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC states its mission is to 'promote and restore responsibility and decency to the entertainment industry in answer to America's demand for positive, family-oriented television programming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mission frames all of PTC's evaluations: emphasis on 'responsibility', 'decency', and 'family-oriented' programming across television, music, movies, and video games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared responsibility: industry and sponsors share responsibility with parents
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC believes the entertainment industry—and its sponsors—share responsibility with parents for children's television viewing habits and therefore should be held accountable for content children can access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC interprets this as justification for pressuring networks, advertisers, and lawmakers to limit children's exposure to perceived harmful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content disqualifier: 'gratuitous' sex, violence, and profanity
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC identifies programs as objectionable when they contain a perceived 'gratuitous' amount of sex, violence, or profanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a qualitative standard in PTC reports and complaints; examples cited include criticism of MTV, BET, and specific music videos and TV episodes. PTC has repeatedly singled out sexualized performances and videos (e.g., Miley Cyrus) and violent or profane scenes as grounds for criticism or complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement of adult content frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC (and PTC-funded studies) measure occurrences of adult-themed content (sex, violence, profanity) quantitatively—for example, reporting 'adult content ... once every 38 seconds' in certain programming—to support claims that children are being exposed too frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These frequency metrics are used in reports (e.g., 'The Rap on Rap') to urge advertisers to withdraw sponsorships and to substantiate complaint filings or public campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of existing ratings systems (TV Parental Guidelines / V-chip)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC contends that the TV Parental Guidelines and V-chip are inaccurate and set low standards; PTC historically applied stricter ratings (e.g., twice as likely to give the toughest 'red light' rating compared to the Guidelines' TV-14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTC's criticisms justify calls for alternate approaches: either stricter enforcement, reworking the guidelines, or replacing/applementing the V-chip system. PTC has publicly labeled the V-chip campaign a failure and contested the official ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy proposal: cable 'a la carte' choice and applying broadcast decency standards to cable
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC supports 'a la carte' cable services allowing families to choose and pay only for channels appropriate for their children, and urges that cable channels be subject to the same decency standards as broadcast television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy stance motivated support for legislation (Family and Consumer Choice Act of 2007) and public campaigns (HowCableShouldBe.com). It's presented as a structural remedy, not just content labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seal of Approval: awarding family-friendly programming
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC awards a 'Seal of Approval' to networks or programs deemed family-friendly for original programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include awarding Disney Channel and Hallmark Channel; the Seal functions as a positive evaluative mark to contrast with the PTC's negative lists and complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advertiser pressure and sponsorship withdrawal as enforcement criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC urges advertisers to withdraw sponsorship of programs it deems inappropriate for children (e.g., campaigns against programs on BET, MTV) as a mechanism to influence programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic is supported by PTC studies alleging frequent adult content in programs aimed at young audiences and is part of a broader strategy that targets economic levers (advertisers) rather than only regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy and complaint-based enforcement tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC's operational criteria include filing FCC complaints, lobbying Congress, publishing 'Top 10 Best & Worst' lists, issuing E-alerts to supporters, urging local preemption of programs, and public statements to pressure networks and regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural actions are treated by PTC as legitimate methods to enforce decency standards; the page documents many specific instances (FCC complaints, calls for investigations, public campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending decency standards to other platforms (in-flight video, internet comments, radio, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC sought guidelines beyond broadcast TV—e.g., in-flight-video guidelines—and has criticized content across multiple media (radio plays, online video comments), implying the same decency criteria should apply broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents a broadened scope for the same family-friendly standard: where children can be exposed, PTC argues for the application of its decency criteria or for platform-specific regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting specific content types (music videos, award show performances, advertising) for youth exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC singles out music videos, televised award-show performances, and certain ads as problematic when they target or reach younger viewers with sexualized or profane content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the page include campaigns against Britney Spears, Miley Cyrus, Rihanna, and Adam Lambert performances; PTC has warned radio stations and advertisers when songs/performances contain obscenities or sexually explicit imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-facing ratings/lists as an accountability tool
rubrics_metrics.description: PTC produces public lists (e.g., 'Top 10 Best and Worst Shows', weekly 'Best and Worst Family TV Shows') to rate network programming and to educate/guide parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lists function as both consumer guidance and advocacy tools; they reflect PTC's evaluative judgments and are used to spotlight content that PTC believes parents should avoid or support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for press and report framing (accusations of slanted reporting vs. PTC's framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: While not a PTC criterion per se, the article documents critiques that PTC's own reporting has been accused of inaccuracy and ideological slant; this highlights an implicit standard for evidentiary rigor and impartiality that PTC is criticized for failing to meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics allege PTC focuses on adult-targeted shows, uses selective examples, or misrepresents research (e.g., criticisms of V-chip reporting). This functions as an external evaluative criterion about the credibility of watchdog reports.
